solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Norm and Jill falling out — it could cause terrible battering

indicators.note: people falling out quarrel and part, so the letters of the two names break apart and regroup

explanation.surface: A couple named Norm and Jill fall out, and the row could end in a terrible beating.
explanation.walkthrough: MJOLLNIR is the hammer of Thor in Norse myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Thor's hammer is a weapon that would deliver a fearsome pounding, so it is something that could cause battering.

clue.text: Sort of poker — girl holds it up, wanton rig

indicators.note: to hold something is to have it in your grasp, so the girl's word wraps round what follows
in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top
wanton means unruly and undisciplined, so the letters run wild into a new order

explanation.surface: A shady card game: a girl props up a crooked rigged table.
explanation.walkthrough: The girl's word splits after its third letter to take in both inner pieces. 'wanton' reads as describing the girl but scrambles the following word.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistigris is a poker variant played with a joker or blank card that serves as a wild card.

clue.text: Lecture: how surprising, short one, and in German forsooth! (6, two words)

indicators.note: something short is cut off before its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: to jaw is to lecture or harangue
'one' means another such exclamation: la, an old cry of surprise, as in 'la, sir!'

explanation.surface: Someone reacts to a lecture with astonished German exclamations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' stands for another word of the same kind as 'how surprising', so it is a second exclamation, la, cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Jawohl is German for 'yes indeed', matching the old English emphatic forsooth.

clue.text: A clumsy person

blocks.note: read plainly: an awkward, lumbering oaf
the setter's reading is the same: this is a bare definition with no wordplay

explanation.walkthrough: This is Azed's competition word: it is given only a plain definition, and readers send in their own cryptic clues for it, so there is no wordplay to find.
explanation.definitionFit: Lob is a dialect word for a lout or lubber, a clumsy, heavy-footed fellow.

clue.text: Church window maybe, unclear if damaged

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so the word's letters are broken up and reset

explanation.surface: A stained-glass window is hard to make out because it has been damaged.
explanation.definitionFit: A lucarne is a dormer or small opening window, often found in a church spire, so a church window is one example.

clue.text: New relocation of city, awkward — it involves movement of plants

indicators.note: a relocation moves things to new places, so the letters of the town word are set down in a fresh order

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
a nasty situation is an awkward one

explanation.surface: Moving to a new city proves awkward, like uprooting a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Nyctinasty is the nightly movement of plant parts, such as leaves folding at dusk, in response to darkness.

clue.text: Poet's scratched some extra stanzas

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

blocks.note: the letters straddling the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A poet crossed out some surplus verses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poet's' marks a Spenserian word: RAST is his past participle of rase, to scratch or erase.
explanation.definitionFit: Rase meant to scrape or graze, so its old poetic past form rast means scratched.

clue.text: Amateur swimmers heading for raised sandbanks

indicators.note: a heading is what goes at the top, so only the opening letter of the next word is kept

blocks.note: the ASA was the Amateur Swimming Association

explanation.surface: Novice swimmers make for some sandbanks that rise out of the water.
explanation.walkthrough: The Amateur Swimming Association, the ASA, governed swimming in England.
explanation.definitionFit: Asar are long glacial ridges of sand and gravel, eskers, so sandbanks is a loose description.

clue.text: Extreme egotism always consumes a Latin tutor oddly

indicators.note: to consume is to take in and swallow, so the first word goes round the rest
done oddly means done in a strange way, so these letters come out in a strange order

blocks.note: ay (or aye) is an old word for always
L is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: A conceited person is forever eating up a Latin teacher in an odd way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ay' is an old poetic word for always. 'oddly' could suggest taking alternate letters, but here it scrambles them.
explanation.definitionFit: Autolatry is worship of oneself, which is egotism carried to its extreme.

clue.text: Pug rolls up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

explanation.surface: A pug dog curls up in a ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A pug nose is short and turned up, which is exactly what a snub nose is.

clue.text: Summon one to appear in court held by person of distinction

indicators.note: a witness appearing in court stands inside it, so one piece goes within another
something held by a person is enclosed in their grasp, so the combined piece goes inside

blocks.note: an ace is an expert, someone outstanding
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A notable figure is called to give evidence in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one to appear in court' reads as a witness, but it is the numeral placed inside an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To accite is an old word for to summon or cite someone to appear.

clue.text: Joy in poetry unknown in the States? Shock admitting that

indicators.note: in places the unknown inside the country's abbreviation
to admit is to let in, so the shock word lets the rest inside it

blocks.note: to jounce is to jolt or bump

explanation.surface: An American is shocked to learn that poetic joy is unheard of in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that' refers back to the whole phrase before the question mark, which goes in as one unit. 'Joy in poetry' signals a Spenserian word.
explanation.definitionFit: Jouysaunce is Spenser's spelling of jouissance, meaning joy or delight, so it is a poetic word for joy.

clue.text: Short wave hits sailor — here's something to dry decks

blocks.note: SW is the abbreviation for short wave

explanation.surface: A sailor is knocked over by a small wave and needs a mop for the deck.
explanation.definitionFit: A swab is a mop used on board ship to clean and dry the decks.

clue.text: Medicinal alkaloid in soft food I fed to one French writer

indicators.note: food fed to someone goes inside them, so the letter goes inside the writer's name

blocks.note: pap is mushy food for babies or invalids

explanation.surface: A medicine is slipped into baby food and given to a French author.
explanation.definitionFit: Papaverine is an alkaloid derived from the opium poppy and used in medicine to relax smooth muscle.

clue.text: End of dirk pierces back — such a one did for Duncan?

definitions.text: such a one did for Duncan?

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, the only one kept here
going back means the letters so far are read in the opposite direction

explanation.surface: A dagger's point goes into someone's back, the kind of blow that killed Duncan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like the body part being pierced, but it reverses the letters. A stuck is Shakespeare's word for a sword thrust, and Macbeth stabbed King Duncan.
explanation.definitionFit: A stuck is an old word for a thrust or stab, the kind of blow that killed King Duncan in Macbeth.

clue.text: Musical work in two acts composed round one of seven advent anthems?

indicators.note: to compose is to arrange material into a new piece, so the letters are rearranged
round means surrounding, so the scrambled letters go about the single letter

blocks.note: the seven Advent antiphons each begin with O, so are known as the O antiphons

explanation.surface: A piece of music in two acts is written around a Christmas-season anthem.
explanation.walkthrough: The O antiphons are seven Latin anthems sung before Christmas, each opening with 'O'.
explanation.definitionFit: A toccata is a piece of music, usually for keyboard, written to show off the player's touch and speed.

clue.text: Charles losing head in execution wretchedly, and come a real cropper

indicators.note: losing something means it is gone, so that letter is taken out of the name
the head of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is used
done wretchedly means done badly, so these letters end up in a mangled order

blocks.note: first letter, the one removed from the name

explanation.surface: King Charles I, beheaded at his execution, came a dreadful cropper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing head' suggests beheading Charles, but the head lost is the first letter of execution.
explanation.definitionFit: To crash-land is to bring an aircraft down hard in an emergency, an idiomatically real cropper or heavy fall.

clue.text: Concerned with carriage seat that shifts with time, yielding on the outside

indicators.note: something that shifts moves about, so the letters move into a new order
being on the outside means wrapping round, so the yielding word encloses the rest

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A carriage seat that moves over time and gives way at the edges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carriage' suggests a coach, but here it means carrying young in the womb.
explanation.definitionFit: Gestation is the carrying of young before birth, so gestative relates to that carriage.

clue.text: Dance? Roller I put in, before I departed, to get hair to stand up

definitions.text: to get hair to stand up

indicators.note: putting something in means inserting it, so the car and letter go inside the dance

blocks.note: a hop is an informal dance
a Roller is slang for a Rolls-Royce, abbreviated RR
the late means the dead, the departed

explanation.surface: At a dance, a hair roller goes in so the hair will stand up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roller' suggests a hair curler, but it is British slang for a Rolls-Royce car. 'departed' means dead, as in 'the late king'.
explanation.definitionFit: To horripilate is to have the hairs rise on the skin, as in goose bumps from fear or cold.

clue.text: General intelligence reversed trouble in brain tissue

indicators.note: something reversed is turned to face the other way, so the next word is read backwards

blocks.note: psychologists call general intelligence the g factor

explanation.surface: Low intelligence is traced back to a problem in the brain's tissue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General intelligence' looks like an IQ phrase; it is the psychologist's g.
explanation.definitionFit: Glia are the supporting cells of the nervous system, making up much of the material of the brain.

clue.text: A garden was ill-tended? Warn these gnomes perhaps

indicators.note: 'Warn these' presents the anagram as the sum of two parts, so one part is taken away to leave the other
an ill-tended garden is in disarray, so its letters are disordered

blocks.note: letters to be taken away from the fodder

explanation.surface: A neglected garden, where the gnome statues might issue a warning.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the letters of A GARDEN WAS rearrange into WARN plus the answer. 'gnomes' suggests garden ornaments but means sayings.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnome is a pithy maxim or aphorism, so adages are examples of such sayings.

clue.text: Britannica no longer with us, in short? What's moral?

blocks.clueFragment: no longer with us, in short

blocks.note: the Encyclopaedia Britannica, shortened to ency.

explanation.surface: Is the old encyclopedia now defunct, and what counts as right anyway?
explanation.walkthrough: 'in short' does double duty, telling you to shorten both encyclopedia and deceased.
explanation.definitionFit: Decency is conduct that conforms to accepted standards of moral behaviour, so it is what is moral.

clue.text: Body of water dried up, its parts being repositioned (6, two words)

indicators.note: the two halves of the word swap places, so front part and back part trade positions

explanation.surface: A stretch of water has dried out and its pieces have shifted about.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Sea is the inlet of the Indian Ocean between Africa and Arabia, a large body of water.

clue.text: Wound once displayed by Marengo regular, losing outer parts?

indicators.note: the answer is on display within the phrase that follows, not built from it
stripping away the outside of the phrase leaves only a run of its inner letters

blocks.note: the inner letters after the outer parts are dropped

explanation.surface: An old wound shown by a soldier at the Battle of Marengo who has lost limbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' marks an archaic word: Spenser's engore means to gore or wound. Marengo was Napoleon's 1800 victory.
explanation.definitionFit: Engore is an obsolete verb meaning to pierce or gore, which is to wound.

clue.text: Rarely drunk, displaying health (except for heart)

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so the middle letter is removed

blocks.note: drinking someone's health is a toast

explanation.surface: A seldom-drinking person raises a glass to someone's health, heartlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rarely' marks an archaic form: tost is the old past participle of toss, which can mean to drink off.
explanation.definitionFit: To toss off a drink is to down it, and tost is a rare old form of tossed, so it means drunk.

clue.text: Tiny coin — I dropped it in Glaswegian drain

indicators.note: something dropped is let go, so that letter falls out of the short word
in places what is left inside the drain word

blocks.note: siver or syver is a Scots word for a street drain

explanation.surface: A small coin slips from someone's hand and falls into a Glasgow gutter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glaswegian' marks a Scots word: a siver or syver is a street gutter drain. The natural move is to put I in the drain; it is the remainder of the short word that goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiver was a small Dutch coin, and the word came to mean any coin of trifling value.

clue.text: He isn't bothered with reversing widow's entitlement, being part of the plot (11, three words)

indicators.note: being bothered means being agitated, so these letters are stirred into a new order
reversing means running backwards, so the following word's letters are read from the end

blocks.note: terce is a Scots legal term for a widow's life-interest in her husband's land

explanation.surface: A man doesn't care about losing his widow's inheritance; perhaps he is in on a scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the secret is to be among those who know about a hidden plan, which means being party to it.

clue.text: Image created by company with trendy clothing

indicators.note: clothing something means dressing it, wrapping it round, so the fashionable word goes about the firm

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A firm's fashionable clothing line builds its public image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothing' looks like garments but is the verb: IN clothes CO.
explanation.definitionFit: An icon is an image or picture, especially a religious painting of a holy figure.

clue.text: All too public 'diary' left in the loo

indicators.note: in places the side abbreviation inside the slang word

blocks.note: bog is British slang for a toilet
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A private diary has been left lying in the toilet for anyone to read.
explanation.definitionFit: A blog is an online journal published for anyone to see, a diary that is far from private.

clue.text: It's unknown for cat to gulp back old coin

indicators.note: to gulp is to swallow, so the cat takes the unknown inside it
going back means the combined letters are read from the end to the start

blocks.note: Tibert is the cat in the Reynard the Fox tales

explanation.surface: A cat swallows an old coin back down without anyone knowing.
explanation.walkthrough: Y goes inside TIBERT after TIB, and the whole is read backwards. A trey bit was the old threepenny piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A treybit, or threepenny bit, was a small coin of pre-decimal British currency worth three old pence.

clue.text: Shop floor official a Liberal? This point is central

blocks.note: a FOC, father of the chapel, is the union official in a printing works
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: Is the union rep a Liberal? That is the key issue.
explanation.walkthrough: A union branch in a British printing works is a chapel, led by its father.
explanation.definitionFit: Something focal is at the focus, the central point of attention or activity.

clue.text: Tribal father against being garlanded?

indicators.note: a garland goes round the wearer, so the short word is wrapped by another

blocks.note: a lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers

explanation.surface: A tribal elder objects to being draped in flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'garlanded' both signals the wrapping and supplies the garland itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Levi was a son of Jacob and the founder of the Israelite tribe of Levites, so he is a tribal patriarch.

clue.text: Argument ma's quit — leaving it involved a giant leap

indicators.note: something that has quit has left, so those letters go

blocks.note: a lemma is a proposition or argument used in a proof

explanation.surface: After a row, mum walks out, which felt like a huge jump.
explanation.walkthrough: The LEM is the Apollo Lunar Excursion Module, from which Armstrong took his 'giant leap for mankind'.
explanation.definitionFit: The lunar module carried Neil Armstrong down to the Moon, the giant leap of his famous first words.

clue.text: Part of speech backing declaration? It's very noticeable

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the abbreviation's letters run the other way

blocks.note: a pronoun is one of the grammatical parts of speech

explanation.surface: A grammar point supports a formal statement and stands out clearly.
explanation.definitionFit: Pronounced means strongly marked or distinct, so a pronounced feature is very noticeable.

clue.text: Courteous old duke supporting woman (endearingly?)

indicators.note: a support goes underneath or behind, so the title abbreviation is placed after the woman

blocks.note: hen is an affectionate address to a woman
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: A gallant old duke props up a lady he is fond of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old' marks hend as an obsolete word; 'hen' is a fond address to a woman, especially in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Hend is an obsolete adjective meaning gracious or courteous, so 'Courteous old' points to it.

clue.text: Mary's delirious in victory — she wears the trousers, figuratively (8, two words)

indicators.note: someone delirious is wildly confused, so the letters of the name are jumbled
in places the scrambled name inside the word for victory

blocks.note: gree is a Scots and archaic word for victory or prize

explanation.surface: Mary is ecstatic after winning; clearly she is the boss at home.
explanation.walkthrough: From the proverb 'the grey mare is the better horse', a wife who rules her husband.
explanation.definitionFit: The grey mare is an idiom for a wife who dominates her husband, the one who wears the trousers.
